02 / What the shader is doing

The building photograph provides the colors. The swirl JPEG map is sampled by the shader as it estimates multiple directions and estimates where its color changes most strongly. That direction approximates a local gradient normal; rotating it by 90 degrees gives a tangent that follows the guide image's contours.

1. Estimate directionCompare pairs of samples around each pixel in the swirl guide. Keep the direction with the strongest color difference.
2. Filter along the tangentSample the building photograph along the contour direction and combine those colors with Gaussian-like weights.
3. Blend and stylizeBlend the filtered result with the original image, then optionally apply pixelation.

What the sliders control

  • Flow / swirl strength changes the blend between the original and filtered image.
  • Filter length changes the number of samples used in the directional filter.
  • Pixelation snaps the source texture coordinates to a coarser grid.

04 / Reference notes

The implementation uses directional filtering and image-gradient examples. The guide image's strongest local color change is treated as an approximate gradient direction, then rotated to obtain a contour-following tangent.

Primary class reference

Ergun Akleman, professor-provided shader examples. The first example reads a control image and uses its red channel as an angle to build a direction vector. The second example estimates an image-gradient direction by comparing samples in multiple directions, rotates the gradient into a tangent, and filters along that tangent. This project follows the second strategy because the chosen swirl JPEG is an ordinary image rather than an angle-encoded vector map.
